title: The loops: cerebellum, basal ganglia and gait
description: How the cerebellum and basal ganglia shape movement without powering it, how to localize ataxia and involuntary movements, and why gait is the best single test.
why: These circuits do not weaken; they shape movement, and gait is where they show.
objectives: Explain why cerebellar and basal ganglia disease spare strength, and check strength before calling a movement ataxic.
Localize cerebellar signs by side and by midline versus hemisphere.
Work through acute ataxia in a child in order of danger and likelihood.
Describe involuntary movements precisely, and read a gait as a tour of the levels of the neuraxis.

sections.title: Modulators, not motors
sections.content:
Two great circuits in the brain move nothing directly. Neither the cerebellum nor the basal ganglia sends its own fibres to the anterior horn cells. Both work in loops: they take in what the cortex intends and what the body reports, and they send their verdict back, through the thalamus, to the motor cortex that will act on it. Pearl calls the cerebellum "the great modulator of the nervous system" (Pearl 2014, p. 116), and the phrase fits the basal ganglia too. One loop tunes accuracy and timing; the other sets how much movement is allowed and how fast.

**Why this changes the exam**

Because these loops shape movement rather than power it, their disease leaves **strength intact**. The cerebellar patient is clumsy, overshoots, and walks on a broad base, but pushes against your hand normally. The basal ganglia patient has too little movement or too much of the wrong kind, but no paralysis. That gives you a rule worth stating plainly: before you call a movement ataxic or dystonic, prove the limb is strong. A weak arm misses the target too, and a weak child falls too. The [[m03-first-fork|first fork]] comes first.

**Two kinds of wrong movement**

- **Cerebellar**: errors in range, rate and rhythm. Dysmetria on finger-nose, irregular rapid alternating movements, an intention tremor that grows as the hand approaches the target, a wide-based gait, nystagmus, and scanning speech (Pearl 2014, pp. 63, 116).
- **Basal ganglia**: errors in amount and selection. Slowness and rigidity at one end; chorea, dystonia, tics and other unwanted movements at the other.

A practical tell: cerebellar tremor appears on action and worsens near the target; a tremor at rest belongs to the basal ganglia.

**In a child**

Clumsiness is one of the commonest reasons a child is referred, and most clumsy children have neither a cerebellar nor a basal ganglia lesion. The developmental exam asks a different question first: is this clumsiness for age? The toddler's broad-based, jerky, falling gait is normal at the age when walking begins (DeMyer, p. 338). Localization starts only when a sign is abnormal for the child in front of you.
keyPoints: The cerebellum and basal ganglia work in loops back to the motor cortex; they shape movement but do not power it.
Their disease spares strength: prove the limb is strong before you call a movement ataxic or dystonic.
Cerebellar errors are of range, rate and rhythm; basal ganglia errors are of amount and selection.
Action tremor worsening near the target is cerebellar; tremor at rest is basal ganglia.

question.question: A 7-year-old overshoots badly on finger-nose testing with the right arm. Strength in that arm is 3 out of 5, with brisk right reflexes. What is the most defensible description?
options: Right cerebellar ataxia; image the posterior fossa
Right arm weakness of upper motor neuron type; the overshoot cannot be called cerebellar while the limb is this weak
question.explanation: Coordination can only be judged in a limb strong enough to perform the task. With power of 3 out of 5 and brisk reflexes, the arm has an upper motor neuron weakness, and that alone can make movements inaccurate. Calling it cerebellar would send you to the wrong level of the neuraxis. Chorea is a random, flowing extra movement, not overshoot on a target task. Normal clumsiness for age does not come with weakness and brisk reflexes on one side.

sections.title: The cerebellum: same side, midline or hemisphere
sections.content:
The cerebellum has its own localizing rules, and the first is the one that surprises students: **cerebellar signs are on the same side as the lesion** (Pearl 2014, p. 63). A unilateral cerebellar lesion causes only ipsilateral cerebellar signs (DeMyer, p. 339).

**Why the same side**

The answer is a double crossing. Cerebellar output leaves through the superior cerebellar peduncle and crosses in the midbrain to reach the opposite thalamus and motor cortex. That cortex then sends its corticospinal tract down, crossing again in the medulla, back to the side where the cerebellum began. Two crossings cancel. A lesion anywhere on that outflow path below the second crossing shows its clumsiness on the side of the cerebellum that started it.

**Midline or hemisphere**

The second rule maps the cerebellum from medial to lateral. The midline vermis and flocculonodular lobe look after the trunk, stance and eye movements; the hemispheres plan and tune the limbs (Pearl 2014, p. 63). So:

- **Midline lesions** give truncal ataxia: axial unsteadiness and a wide-based, staggering gait, with little ataxia of the limbs when tested lying down (Brazis 2011, pp. 411-412), and often nystagmus, vertigo, nausea and vomiting (Pearl 2014, p. 63).
- **Hemispheric lesions** give limb ataxia on the same side: dysmetria, intention tremor and poor rapid alternating movements (Brazis 2011, p. 412).
- **Both at once**, a pancerebellar syndrome, suggests something diffuse: a toxin or drug, a metabolic or inherited disorder, or multiple sclerosis (DeMyer, p. 339).

**A correction worth making**

Some teaching texts say cerebellar output is all inhibitory; Pearl does (Pearl 2014, p. 63). The cerebellar cortex's own output, from the Purkinje cells to the deep nuclei, is inhibitory. But the deep nuclei, which carry the cerebellum's message to the rest of the brain, are excitatory in all their projections except those to the inferior olive (Brazis 2011, p. 405). The difference matters if you want to understand why a cerebellar lesion leaves the motor cortex under-driven rather than released.

**In a child**

The caudal vermis syndrome, staggering with relatively spared limbs, is typical of a medulloblastoma, the classic midline tumour of childhood (Brazis 2011, p. 412). A child who walks badly but performs heel-shin well lying down has told you the lesion is in the middle.
keyPoints: Cerebellar signs are on the same side as the lesion (Pearl 2014, p. 63); two crossings cancel.
Midline lesions give truncal and gait ataxia with relatively spared limbs; hemispheric lesions give same-side limb ataxia (Brazis 2011, pp. 411-412).
Bilateral, pancerebellar signs suggest a diffuse cause: toxin, drug, metabolic, inherited or demyelinating (DeMyer, p. 339).
The deep nuclei carry cerebellar output and are excitatory except to the inferior olive (Brazis 2011, p. 405); only the Purkinje stage before them is inhibitory.

question.question: A 5-year-old has a month of morning vomiting and now staggers and sways when standing, on a broad base. Lying down, finger-nose and heel-shin are nearly normal on both sides. Where is the lesion most likely to be?
options: The cerebellar vermis in the midline
The dorsal columns of the spinal cord
question.explanation: Ataxia of stance and gait with relatively spared limb coordination is the midline, truncal pattern; with morning vomiting it raises the possibility of a midline posterior fossa tumour blocking the fourth ventricle, such as a medulloblastoma (Brazis 2011, p. 412). A right hemispheric lesion would show right limb ataxia on testing. Dorsal column disease causes a sensory ataxia that worsens with the eyes closed and comes with lost position sense, which was not described. Bilateral hemispheric disease would bring weakness, reflex changes or cognitive signs rather than isolated truncal ataxia.

sections.title: Acute ataxia in a child
sections.content:
A child who could walk yesterday and staggers today is one of the commonest urgent problems in child neurology, and it is a good test of whether you can think in levels and tempos at the same time. The level is usually the cerebellum or its connections. The tempo, acute, narrows the mechanisms to a short list that you can walk through in order of danger and of likelihood.

**The short list**

- **An ingestion.** A toddler with sudden ataxia and drowsiness has taken something until proved otherwise; many sedatives and antiseizure drugs cause a pancerebellar picture.
- **Post-infectious cerebellar ataxia.** An immune-mediated ataxia after a viral illness; Pearl lists it among the infectious causes of cerebellar disease (Pearl 2014, p. 63). The child is alert, the ataxia is mostly truncal, and the rest of the exam is normal.
- **Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia.** Chaotic, darting, multidirectional eye movements and jerks of the trunk and limbs in an irritable child. This pattern is a reason to look for a neuroblastoma.
- **A posterior fossa tumour.** Usually a story of weeks rather than days, often with headache and vomiting from raised intracranial pressure (Brazis 2011, p. 412). A child who seems to have become ataxic overnight may have been compensating for longer.
- **Something that is not the cerebellum.** Absent reflexes with ataxia points to the peripheral nerves, as in a variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome; lost position sense points to a sensory ataxia; a weak leg can masquerade as ataxia.

**What to do first**

Assess the level of consciousness and ask, specifically, what medicines and substances are in the house. Then look at the eyes: nystagmus, opsoclonus, and the optic discs for papilloedema. Check the reflexes, position sense and strength, so that the ataxia is truly cerebellar. A child who is drowsy, has papilloedema, focal signs, a severe headache, or is getting worse needs urgent imaging; an alert child with isolated truncal ataxia after a viral illness and a normal exam can often be watched closely.

**The philosophy**

Acute ataxia rewards the discipline of this whole curriculum. The commonest cause is benign, and the temptation is to stop at it. The order of questions (Is this child safe? Is this really the cerebellum? What else keeps it company?) is what finds the ingestion, the tumour and the neuroblastoma.
keyPoints: Acute ataxia in a toddler: think of an ingestion first, especially with drowsiness.
Post-infectious ataxia: alert, truncal, otherwise normal exam, after a viral illness (Pearl 2014, p. 63).
Chaotic multidirectional eye movements with myoclonus suggest opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia: look for a neuroblastoma.
Drowsiness, papilloedema, focal signs or worsening mean urgent imaging.

question.question: A 2-year-old has become unsteady over three days and is irritable. His eyes make rapid, chaotic, conjugate darting movements in all directions, and his trunk and limbs jerk. Reflexes are normal and there was no access to medicines. What should the next step include?
options: Reassurance and review in two weeks for post-infectious ataxia
Nerve conduction studies for a variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome
question.explanation: Chaotic multidirectional darting eye movements (opsoclonus) with myoclonus and ataxia form the opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome, which in a young child should prompt a search for a neuroblastoma. Treating it as simple post-infectious ataxia misses the defining eye sign. A lumbar puncture alone does not look for the tumour that may be driving the syndrome. Normal reflexes argue against a Guillain-Barré variant, and opsoclonus is not part of it.

sections.title: Vertigo: time and company
sections.content:
Vertigo is an illusion of movement, and the first localizing question is whether the illusion starts in the ear and its nerve or in the brainstem and cerebellum that read them. Two coordinates answer it: **time** and **company**.

**Time**

An acute vestibular lesion begins abruptly and then fades as the brain compensates for the lost input (Pearl 2014, p. 119). Peripheral vertigo therefore has a shape: worst at the start, easing over days; Pearl gives vestibular neuronitis four to ten days (Pearl 2014, p. 121). The converse is just as useful. Continuous dizziness that never fluctuates over long periods is not the vestibular pattern (Pearl 2014, p. 119), and it should make you look elsewhere.

**The eyes**

[[m07-brainstem|Module 7]] listed the nystagmus pearls; two carry most of the weight. Fixation suppresses peripheral nystagmus but not central nystagmus, and pure vertical or pure torsional nystagmus is central (Brazis 2011, p. 265). Pearl warns that in the very first hours fixation may not suppress even a peripheral nystagmus (Pearl 2014, p. 120), so look again.

**Company**

Pearl and Emsellem attach their rule, "the company you keep", to central nystagmus (Pearl 2014, p. 121). Hearing loss and tinnitus keep company with the ear (Pearl 2014, p. 119); double vision, slurred speech, facial numbness and limb ataxia keep company with the brainstem and cerebellum. The figure weighs them that way. Tick what you see, and notice that one central feature overrules any number of peripheral ones.

**The mimic that matters**

A cerebellar infarct can closely mimic acute labyrinthitis: vertigo, nausea and vomiting, sometimes with no limb ataxia at all. What betrays it is nystagmus that changes direction, and someone has to look for it (Pearl 2014, pp. 121-122). In children the central cause not to miss is a **posterior fossa tumour**, common in childhood (Pearl 2014, p. 63); Brazis counts posterior fossa tumours, Chiari malformations and cerebellar malformations among the commonest central causes of pediatric dizziness (Brazis 2011, p. 355).

**Recurrent spells in a child**

Brief, recurrent attacks are a different tempo with a different list. Brazis considers vestibular migraine probably the commonest cause of recurrent vertigo in children (Brazis 2011, p. 354). He also describes **benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood**: short spells, sometimes in clusters, in which the child looks frightened, pale and sweaty but stays fully aware, probably a precursor of migraine (Brazis 2011, p. 355). Between spells the child should be normal. If the exam is not normal, the company has changed, and so has the address.
keyPoints: An acute vestibular lesion eases as the brain compensates; unremitting, unfluctuating dizziness is not the vestibular pattern (Pearl 2014, p. 119).
Fixation suppresses peripheral but not central nystagmus; pure vertical or torsional nystagmus is central (Brazis 2011, p. 265).
A cerebellar infarct can mimic labyrinthitis; direction-changing nystagmus gives it away (Pearl 2014, pp. 121-122).
In children, a posterior fossa tumour is the central cause not to miss (Pearl 2014, p. 63; Brazis 2011, p. 355).
Brief recurrent spells with a normal exam between: vestibular migraine or benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood (Brazis 2011, pp. 354-355).

question.question: A 7-year-old has had three days of vertigo and vomiting after a cold. Hearing is normal and finger-nose is accurate. Her nystagmus beats to the left on left gaze and to the right on right gaze. What should you do?
options: Diagnose vestibular neuritis and expect recovery within days
Perform a positional manoeuvre for benign positional vertigo
Reassure the family that this is benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood
Treat it as central and image the posterior fossa
question.explanation: Nystagmus that changes direction with gaze is central, and it is exactly the sign that separates a cerebellar lesion from a labyrinthitis that it otherwise mimics (Pearl 2014, pp. 121-122); in a child the posterior fossa tumour is the cause to exclude (Pearl 2014, p. 63). Vestibular neuritis is the tempting reading after a cold, and normal limb coordination makes it more tempting, but its nystagmus beats one way only (Pearl 2014, p. 120), and limb ataxia can be absent in a cerebellar infarct too (Pearl 2014, p. 122). A positional manoeuvre does not explain constant gaze-dependent nystagmus. Benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood comes in brief, recurrent spells, not three continuous days (Brazis 2011, p. 355).

sections.title: The basal ganglia: too little or too much
sections.content:
If the cerebellum asks "how accurately?", the basal ganglia ask "how much, and which one?" Their disorders fall on a single axis, and Pearl uses it to sort the whole field: **hypokinetic** disorders with too little movement, and **hyperkinetic** disorders with movements that should not be there (Pearl 2014, p. 116).

**Two ends of the axis**

- **Too little**: slowness, cogwheel rigidity, a tremor at rest, and a stooped, shuffling gait that cannot easily stop (Pearl 2014, p. 116). This is the adult Parkinson picture, and it is rare in childhood.
- **Too much**: chorea (brief, random, flowing movements that dart from one body part to another), dystonia (sustained or repeated twisting postures, often provoked by a particular action), tics, myoclonus and athetosis. In children this end of the axis dominates.

**Why the involuntary movement is the localizing sign**

There is no weakness to measure and often no reflex change, so the movement itself carries the address. Chorea, dystonia and a tremor at rest place the lesion in the subcortex and deep grey matter, the one level where the [[m03-first-fork|localizer]] keeps them. The skill is in describing the movement precisely before naming it: what part moves, whether it is brief or sustained, random or patterned, at rest or on action, suppressible or not.

**Sydenham chorea**

The classic childhood example is Sydenham chorea, a post-streptococcal disorder that Pearl calls pathognomonic of acute rheumatic fever (Pearl 2014, p. 116). A school-aged child becomes fidgety and clumsy, drops things, cannot keep the tongue protruded, and grips with a waxing and waning squeeze; behaviour and mood often change too. The localization is the basal ganglia; the diagnosis obliges you to look for the rest of rheumatic fever, including the heart.

**Other childhood patterns**

Dystonia that fluctuates through the day, dyskinetic cerebral palsy after injury to the deep grey matter around birth, and movement disorders that arrive with regression all point to the same level but to very different mechanisms. The level is the beginning of the reasoning, not the end; [[m11-where-to-what|tempo]] will divide them.
keyPoints: Basal ganglia disorders sit on one axis: hypokinetic (too little movement) or hyperkinetic (unwanted movement) (Pearl 2014, p. 116).
In children the hyperkinetic end dominates: chorea, dystonia, tics, myoclonus.
Describe the movement precisely (which part, brief or sustained, random or patterned, rest or action) before naming it.
Sydenham chorea is post-streptococcal and pathognomonic of acute rheumatic fever: look for the rest of the disease (Pearl 2014, p. 116).

question.question: A 9-year-old girl has three weeks of fidgety, irregular movements flitting between her hands, face and feet, a fluctuating hand grip, and new tearfulness. She had a sore throat six weeks ago. Strength and reflexes are normal. After placing the lesion in the basal ganglia, what is the most important next step?
options: Look for the other features of acute rheumatic fever, including the heart
Reassure the family that this is a tic disorder
question.explanation: Random, flowing movements that move from one body part to another are chorea, and after a recent sore throat Sydenham chorea is the leading cause; Pearl calls it pathognomonic of acute rheumatic fever (Pearl 2014, p. 116). Diagnosing it obliges you to look for carditis and the rest of the disease. The cord cannot generate chorea. Tics are patterned, repetitive and briefly suppressible, unlike these flitting movements, and calling it a tic disorder would miss the heart. Nerve studies examine the motor unit, which is not the level here.

sections.title: Gait as the integrator
sections.content:
If you could watch a child do only one thing, walking would be the choice. Gait is an excellent screen of the whole motor system (Pearl 2014, p. 114), and lesions at each level of the neuraxis impair it in a characteristic way, so the features of the gait suggest the lesion location and its probable cause (DeMyer, p. 338). Pearl teaches it from the bottom up, from muscle to cortex (Pearl 2014, pp. 114-117), which turns the gait into a tour of the eleven levels.

**Bottom up**

- **Muscle**: a waddling, sway-backed gait from weak hip muscles; the classic boy with Duchenne dystrophy has big calves, lordosis and a waddle (Pearl 2014, p. 115).
- **Junction**: a gait that fatigues and recovers with rest.
- **Nerve**: a steppage gait, lifting the knee high to clear a dropped foot.
- **Root**: an antalgic gait, avoiding weight on a painful leg.
- **Cord**: a stiff, scissoring gait from spasticity.
- **Basal ganglia**: a dancing, choreic gait, or a shuffling one.
- **Cerebellum**: a wide-based gait that cannot manage heel to toe.
- **Hemisphere**: a circumducting gait, the stiff leg swung outward.

Use the figure above to pick a gait and see the level it points to and the company it keeps.

**The developing gait**

A child's gait has its own timetable. The newborn steps reflexly when held upright; cruising follows; around the first birthday the toddler walks freely on a broad base with short, jerky steps and frequent falls, and only later develops the mature heel-toe stride with swinging arms (DeMyer, p. 338). A broad-based, falling gait is a sign at five and normal at thirteen months.

**Toe walking**

Toe walking is the best example of a gait that does not localize on its own. It can be the first sign of Duchenne dystrophy or of spastic diplegia, it is common in autism, and in a child who runs, skips and hops normally it may be an idiosyncratic, sometimes familial pattern with no disease at all (DeMyer, p. 338). The rest of the exam decides.

**How to look**

Ask the child to walk, run, walk on the heels and on the toes, and walk heel to toe. Heel and toe walking test the muscles of the sciatic territory as well as balance (DeMyer, p. 338). Make it a race or a game.
keyPoints: Gait screens the whole motor system; its features suggest the level and the cause (DeMyer, p. 338; Pearl 2014, p. 114).
Bottom up: waddle (muscle), fatigable (junction), steppage (nerve), antalgic (root), scissoring (cord), choreic (basal ganglia), wide-based (cerebellum), circumducting (hemisphere).
A broad-based, falling toddler gait is normal around the first birthday (DeMyer, p. 338).
Toe walking does not localize alone: Duchenne dystrophy, spastic diplegia, autism, or an idiopathic familial pattern (DeMyer, p. 338).

question.question: A 4-year-old is referred for toe walking. He runs, skips, hops on either foot and can stand flat-footed. He rises from the floor without using his hands, his calves are normal in size, and reflexes and plantars are normal. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Spastic diplegia from periventricular white-matter injury
An idiosyncratic or familial toe-walking pattern without neurological disease
question.explanation: Toe walking needs the rest of the exam to localize. A child who runs, skips and hops normally, rises without a Gowers manoeuvre and has normal tone and reflexes has none of the serious causes, and DeMyer describes exactly this child as having an idiosyncratic, sometimes familial gait (DeMyer, p. 338). Duchenne dystrophy would usually show proximal weakness and calf enlargement. Spastic diplegia would bring increased tone and brisk reflexes in the legs. A neuropathy tends to cause foot drop and a steppage gait, the opposite of toe walking.

quiz.question: A 12-year-old has a coarse tremor of the right hand that is absent at rest and grows larger as her finger approaches your finger. Which level does this tremor point to?
options: The right cerebellar hemisphere or its outflow
quiz.explanation: A tremor that appears on action and worsens near the target is an intention tremor, a cerebellar sign. Cerebellar signs are on the same side as the lesion, so a right hand tremor points to the right cerebellar hemisphere or its outflow. A basal ganglia tremor is typically present at rest. A left cerebellar lesion would affect the left limbs. A median nerve lesion causes weakness and numbness, not an intention tremor.

quiz.question: A 15-year-old started a new antiseizure medicine a week ago and is now unsteady, with slurred speech, nystagmus in every direction of gaze, and ataxia of all four limbs. Which reading fits best?
options: A pancerebellar syndrome from a drug effect
A lesion of the left medial longitudinal fasciculus
quiz.explanation: Bilateral, symmetric cerebellar signs make a pancerebellar syndrome, which suggests a diffuse cause such as a toxin or drug rather than a focal lesion (DeMyer, p. 339); some antiseizure drugs also cause a central-type nystagmus (Pearl 2014, p. 121). A hemispheric tumour would give same-side limb signs. A midline lesion would spare the limbs more than this. A medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion causes an internuclear ophthalmoplegia, not four-limb ataxia.

quiz.question: A 13-year-old stands steadily with her eyes open but sways and nearly falls when she closes them. Vibration and position sense are lost in the toes, and the ankle reflexes are absent. Finger-nose is accurate. What kind of ataxia is this?
options: Sensory ataxia from the large sensory nerves or dorsal columns
quiz.explanation: Steadiness with the eyes open that fails with the eyes closed is a positive Romberg sign: vision was compensating for lost position sense. With absent vibration and position sense and lost ankle reflexes, this is a sensory ataxia from the large sensory nerves or dorsal columns. The cerebellar patient is unsteady with the eyes open too and more or less passes a Romberg test (DeMyer, p. 339). There is nothing inconsistent or effortful to suggest a functional disorder.

quiz.question: A 10-year-old with high-arched feet lifts both knees high and slaps the feet down when walking. Ankle reflexes are absent and the calves are thin. Which level does the gait point to?
quiz.explanation: Lifting the knees high to clear dropped feet is a steppage gait, the gait of the peripheral nerve (Pearl 2014, p. 115). Bilateral foot drop with high arches, thin calves and absent ankle reflexes suggests a symmetric, length-dependent neuropathy, often inherited, as in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (DeMyer, p. 338). A cerebellar gait is wide-based, not high-stepping. A cord lesion causes a stiff, scissoring gait with brisk reflexes. Muscle disease usually gives a proximal waddle.

quiz.question: Which statement about cerebellar output is accurate?
options: All cerebellar output is inhibitory, so a cerebellar lesion releases the motor cortex
Cerebellar output reaches the opposite cortex without crossing
Purkinje cells inhibit the deep nuclei, and the deep nuclei excite their targets, except the inferior olive
The deep nuclei are inhibitory and the Purkinje cells excitatory
quiz.explanation: The cerebellar cortex speaks only through the Purkinje cells, which inhibit the deep cerebellar nuclei. The deep nuclei then carry the cerebellum's output, and all of their projections are excitatory except those to the inferior olive (Brazis 2011, p. 405). The statement that all output is inhibitory, found in some primers, confuses the Purkinje stage with the final output. The outflow does cross, in the midbrain, which is half of the double crossing that keeps cerebellar signs on the same side. The last option reverses the two stages.

quiz.question: A 13-month-old who started walking three weeks ago walks on a broad base with short, jerky, irregular steps, arms held up and slightly flexed, and falls every few steps. Strength, tone and reflexes are normal. What do you conclude?
options: Midline cerebellar ataxia; image the posterior fossa
A normal toddler gait for age
quiz.explanation: A broad base, short jerky steps, raised arms and frequent falls are the normal toddler gait when independent walking begins, around the first birthday (DeMyer, p. 338). The same gait at five would be a sign; at thirteen months, with a normal exam, it is development. Calling it cerebellar ataxia ignores age. Spastic diplegia would bring stiff legs and brisk reflexes. A myopathy would show weakness and difficulty rising.

quiz.question: A 3-year-old has brief spells every few weeks: she suddenly looks frightened, clings to her mother, turns pale and sweaty, and cannot stand steadily, then is herself again within minutes. She stays responsive throughout. Her examination between spells is normal. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Focal seizures arising from the temporal lobe
quiz.explanation: Brief recurrent spells of vertigo in which a young child looks frightened, pale and sweaty without losing awareness, with a normal exam between them, are the picture Brazis gives for benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood, probably a migraine precursor (Brazis 2011, p. 355). A posterior fossa tumour is the dangerous alternative to keep in mind, but brief spells with full recovery and a normal examination between them are not the picture of a growing mass; a sign that persists between spells would change the answer. Vestibular neuritis is a single episode that eases over days (Pearl 2014, p. 121). Temporal lobe seizures can cause vertigo, but Brazis advises looking for staring, automatisms or other temporal lobe features, which are absent here (Brazis 2011, p. 355).

opener.parable: A loop does not move the limb; it edits the movement. Damage the editor and the sentence is still written, only badly.
opener.history: Gordon Holmes (1876–1965), whose scheme of examination underlies the one neurologists still use, described how a cerebellar patient breaks a movement into pieces, reaching the nose in two separate steps instead of one smooth curve.
